A.explanation: The lamp is connected directly across the cell in parallel with the variable resistor, so the p.d. across the lamp equals the constant e.m.f. and $P = V^2/R$ stays constant.

B.explanation: The lamp is in series with the variable resistor, so changing the resistance changes the circuit current and the lamp power $P = I^2R$.

C.explanation: The lamp is in series with the parallel combination, so changing the variable resistor changes total resistance, total current and hence power in the lamp.

D.explanation: The lamp is in parallel with the variable resistor but that whole combination is in series with a fixed resistor, so the p.d. across the lamp changes when the variable resistor is adjusted.

hints: Look at where the two terminals of the lamp connect in each diagram and whether the variable resistor is in the same series path as the lamp.
Recall lamp power depends on the p.d. across it as $P = V^2/R$, so power is unchanged only if $V$ across the lamp is fixed at the cell e.m.f.
Check which circuit keeps the full cell e.m.f. across the lamp while the variable resistor forms a separate parallel branch with negligible internal resistance.
walkthrough: Identify the lamp and variable resistor connections: in A they are on two separate parallel branches both connected directly across the cell.
State the rule: with negligible internal resistance the terminal p.d. equals the e.m.f. $E$, and any component connected directly across the cell has p.d. $V = E$.
Apply to A: the lamp voltage is $V = E$ regardless of the current in the other branch, so lamp power $P = V^2/R_{lamp} = E^2/R_{lamp}$ is constant.

Contrast with the others: in B the lamp and variable resistor share the same series current, in C the lamp carries the total current of a changing total resistance, and in D the series fixed resistor takes a changing share of $E$.
Therefore only the circuit with the lamp permanently across the constant e.m.f. keeps the same power. This is option A
